title: UNESCO World Heritage: Preserving the Best of Humanity
summary: Hosts Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explain UNESCO's World Heritage program: its origins in post-World War Two preservation efforts and the 1959 Aswan Dam campaign to move Egyptian temples, the 1972 World Heritage Convention and World Heritage List, the World Heritage Committee and fund, natural versus cultural sites, the 2003 intangible cultural heritage list with examples like horseback shrimp fishing in Belgium and Bulgarian bagpipes, the danger list and delisting cases (Congo national parks, Bamiyan Valley, Liverpool, Arabian Oryx Sanctuary), politics and withdrawal by the United States, the Hagia Sophia reconversion in 2020, and a listener mail about the Kowloon Walled City Park.

segments.title: Opening and origins of UNESCO World Heritage
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode, a quick turnaround prompted by a contortionism episode in which Mongolia's bid was turned down. They explain that World Heritage sites remain under national sovereignty but are shared responsibility of humanity.

segments.title: Post-war origins and the Aswan Dam campaign
segments.summary: UNESCO formed in 1945 after World War Two destruction. In 1959 Egypt asked for help with the Aswan Dam reservoir threatening monuments; about eighty million dollars was raised and two temples were moved about 650 feet.

segments.title: World Heritage List, committee, and fund
segments.summary: The 1972 convention created the World Heritage List. The committee has twenty-one elected member countries; members must submit reports and receive funding from the World Heritage Fund, with emergency aid and expert training available. The US has joined and left the body at different times.

segments.title: Natural and cultural site categories
segments.summary: Sites are divided into natural and cultural categories. Serengeti National Park is an example of natural significance for predator-prey interactions; Venice and the Statue of Liberty are cultural examples. Some sites meet several criteria.

segments.title: Site totals, regional distribution, and dark heritage
segments.summary: There are 1,248 World Heritage sites, mostly cultural, with Europe and North America holding about 46 percent. The Navy School of Mechanics in Argentina is preserved as a memory site of dictatorship abuses.

segments.title: Intangible cultural heritage
segments.summary: In 2003 UNESCO added oral traditions, performing arts, and social practices. Examples include horseback shrimp fishing in Belgium, Bulgarian bagpipe making, French baguette making, Finnish sauna culture, Croatian gingerbread, Spanish human towers, Bosnian scythe mowing competition, and Swiss yodeling.

segments.title: Danger list and delisting
segments.summary: Sites can be placed on the Danger List, with ascertained or potential danger, due to war, climate change, or development. Examples include Congo national parks (1994 to 1997), Bamiyan Valley in Afghanistan after the 2001 destruction of Buddha statues, Everglades, Odessa, and Aleppo. Liverpool was delisted in 2021 after stadium construction; the Arabian Oryx Sanctuary in Oman was delisted in 2007.

segments.title: Sites removed from danger list
segments.summary: Countries work to get sites off the danger list; in 2025 three sites were removed, including Gadames in Libya, where improved irrigation lowered the water table. Hosts joke about a crossroads link to Robert Johnson.

segments.title: Politics, tourism, and US withdrawal
segments.summary: Scholar Lynn Meskel is cited saying the list is about political and economic gain. Repatriation and indigenous peoples' exclusion are discussed. The US withdrew from UNESCO in the 1980s and 2018 yet can still nominate sites; blocs of countries vote together.

segments.title: Hagia Sophia reconversion and enforcement
segments.summary: In 2020 Turkish President Erdogan unilaterally converted Hagia Sophia from museum back to mosque, without UNESCO consultation. Hosts note UNESCO had little recourse. The Sydney Opera House is noted as near danger listing due to rising sea levels.

segments.title: More protected examples and closing remarks
segments.summary: Further examples of protected traditions: Mexican Day of the Dead, Peruvian ceviche preparation, Turkmen tiki horse breeding, and midwifery. Hosts joke about food and wrap up the topic.

segments.title: Transition to listener mail
segments.summary: Hosts move on to listener mail.

segments.title: Listener mail: Kowloon Walled City Park
segments.summary: Stephen Cook of Halifax, Nova Scotia describes visiting Kowloon Walled City Park in Hong Kong, its remnants, the museum building, and a streetscape exhibit using sets from the film Twilight of the Warriors: Walled In.
